newsitem.title: UK: Mechanism to warn of jet fuel price changes urged.
newsitem.headline: Mechanism to warn of jet fuel price changes urged.

text.p: The UK Air Freight Forum said it has urged that a mechanism be developed to track jet fuel price fluctuations and alert airlines as to when they may have to impose fuel surcharges on freight rates.
A spokesman told a news briefing that the International Air Transport Association (IATA) would be approached by the Forum to set up the mechanism and recommend its use by member airlines.
He said the aim was for airlines to be sufficiently aware of likely peaks in jet fuel costs.
This would enable them to decide on surcharges and to give ample warning about their introduction to freight forwarders and shippers.
The Forum was formed in November 1996 and is made up of 20 major airlines, freight forwarders and shippers.
"We feel that shippers and agents should be given 30 days' notice of any surcharges," said the British Shippers' Council's (BSC) shipping and air manager, Andrew Traill.

Forum committee member Mark Olney, UK and Ireland cargo manager of Cathay Pacific Airways said this did not happen in late-October/early November 1996 "when the situation could have been handled so much better by the airlines".
He was referring to a time when many airlines around the world rapidly imposed surcharges on air cargo rates to counter rapidly rising fuel costs.
Shippers and forwarders complained that they received little, or in some cases no notice of these surcharges and are anxious to prevent a similar occurrence in future, industry observers say.
Olney said that in the event of future fuel price escalation, airlines should still be able to give their customers a month's warning of any necessary rate rises.
"Last year, the (rising fuel price) trend was seen to be developing for months but the airlines did nothing about it," he said.
"What we want is a mechanism to act as a trigger when fuel prices reach a certain level," allowing airlines to plan rate rises and give ample warning of them to shippers and agents, Olney added.
